extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards from a publishing manual of style covering capitalization, use of small caps, italics, quotations, spelling, and punctuation for preparing publishable text.

rubrics_metrics.name: 50. Capitals and small capitals for dates, salutatory, signatures, and residences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Capitals and Small Capitals for the names of town and state in the date line, the salutatory phrase at the beginning of letters, and the signature and residence at the end of letters or articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set date line to the right with one em indent and preferably in smaller type; salutatory (e.g., 'My dear Mr. Smith:') set flush followed by a colon in same type as body on a separate line; signature and residence set to the right with one em indent in same type as body. Example formats: 'Chicago, Ill., January 1, 1911' ; 'My dear Mr. Smith:' ; 'Charles W. Scott' ; notes on centering address lines in smaller type and caps/small caps for each line.

rubrics_metrics.name: 51. Capitalization in resolutions, notes, and constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions use 'Whereas'; in notes (not footnotes) use 'Note.' followed by a period and a dash; in constitutions and by-laws use 'Section' introducing paragraphs followed by a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First use of 'Section' spelled out; subsequent uses may be abbreviated (e.g., 'Section 1. ...' then 'Sec. 2. ...'). Example: 'Note. — It should be noticed that ....' ; 'Section 1. This association shall be styled ....'

rubrics_metrics.name: 52. Small capitals for abbreviations of time and era
rubrics_metrics.description: Set A.M., P.M., B.C., and A.D. in small capitals without spaces between letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '11:30 A.M.'; '53 B.C., 1906 A.D.'; cross-references to other rules on spacing and usage (see rules 22, 103, 106, 219).

rubrics_metrics.name: 53. Use lower-case initial for words now common derived from proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: Words of common usage originally proper names and their derivatives, and generally verbs derived from proper names, should use a small (lower-case) initial letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Utopia, bohemian, philistine, titanic, platonic, quixotic, bonanza, china, morocco, guinea-pig, boycott, roman (type), italicize, christianize, anglicize, macadamize.' (See cross-ref rule 1.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 54. Lower-case for minor subdivisions in literary references
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case for minor subdivisions and their abbreviations in literary references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note; chap., sec., p., art., vs., l., n.' (See rules 37, 110, 237.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 55. Lower-case for units of measurement abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case abbreviations for units of measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'h. = hour, min. = minute, sec. = second; lb. = pound, oz. = ounce; yd. = yard, ft. = foot; etc.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 56. Italic side-heads capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In italic side-heads, capitalize only the first word and proper names; the rest in lower case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cross-references to rules 172 and 280 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 57. Capitalize first word of a quotation connected to preceding text
rubrics_metrics.description: If a quotation is immediately connected with the preceding text (e.g., through a conjunction), capitalize the first word even if the original begins a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to illustrations and exceptions in rules 35 and 131.

rubrics_metrics.name: 58. Use of italics for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases to lend emphasis or importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This was, however, not the case'; 'It is sufficiently plain that the sciences of life, at least, are studies of processes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 59. Italicize foreign words and brief foreign passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize foreign words/phrases not incorporated into English and (as a rule) single sentences or brief passages in a foreign language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Darwinian Weltanschauung'; 'Napoleon's coup d'état'; 'De gustibus non est disputandum.' Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or names of foreign institutions/places commonly used in English or words that have become anglicized (examples given).

rubrics_metrics.name: 60. Italicize titles of publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize titles of books, plays, essays, cycles of poems, single long poems, pamphlets, treatises, documents, periodicals, and proceedings; include city in newspaper titles if integral to name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Spencer, Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer Night's Dream; the Chicago Tribune, the New York Times.' Note exceptions: some journals use different practices; exceptions for lengthy bibliographies or tables to avoid too many italics; Books of the Bible and ancient manuscripts set in roman.

rubrics_metrics.name: 61. Italicize certain Latin/technical abbreviations in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words commonly used in literary and legal references: ad loc., circa (ca.), et al., ibid., idem, infra, loc. cit., op. cit., passim, sic, supra, s.v., vide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not italicize cf., e.g., i.e., v. (versus), viz., etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 62. Use italics for 'See' and 'See also' in indexes and similar words in errata lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize 'See' and 'See also' for cross-references where differentiation is desirable, and 'for' and 'read' in lists of errata to separate incorrect vs correct readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'See also Sociology; for levee read levée.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 63. Italicize names of plaintiff and defendant in legal citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize the names of plaintiff and defendant in legal case citations and titles of proceedings containing prefixes like in re, ex parte, In the matter of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Conolly v. Union Sewer Pipe Co.; In re Smith; Ex parte Brown; In the matter of the petition of Henry Robinson for a writ of habeas corpus.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 64. Capitalization and setting of address lines and primary address lines in letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Address lines in speeches, reports, and primary address lines in letters should be set flush on a separate line with nouns capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen:'; 'Mr. John Smith, 321 Dearborn Street, Chicago, Ill.,' ; 'Dear Sir: I take pleasure in announcing ....'

rubrics_metrics.name: 65. Formatting of signatures with position or title
rubrics_metrics.description: In signatures, the position or title added after the name follows specific centering/indentation rules depending on length relative to the name, with flexibility for special cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
If position is one word, run into same line as name; if more than one word but not longer than name, center first letter under name and indent one em on right; if longer than name, center name over second line and set title flush. Examples illustrated with 'Arthur P. Maguire, Secretary' and 'Carter H. Harrison
Mayor of Chicago'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 66. Use of a), b), c) for subdivisions and fractional indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a), b), c), etc., to indicate subdivisions (single parenthesis if beginning a paragraph, double if run in) and use letters a, b, c affixed to numbers to denote fractional parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Luke 4:31a.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 67. Letters to designate unknown quantities in technical matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Use letters to designate unknown quantities, lines, etc., in algebraic, geometrical, and similar contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'ac + bc = c(a + b); the lines AB and A'B'; the nth power.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 68. Letters in text referring to illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters in legends or text referring to corresponding letters in accompanying illustrations should be used as a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'At the point A above (see diagram).'

rubrics_metrics.name: 69. Lower-case references to particular letters
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring to specific letters themselves, set them as references: 'the letter u, a small v.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short examples in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: 70. Use abbreviations for shillings and pence after numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 's. d.' (shillings and pence) following numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '35s. 6d.' (See rule 270 cross-ref.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 71. Italicize scientific (Latin) names in zoology, geology, paleontology when genus and species used together
rubrics_metrics.description: In zoological, geological, and paleontological matter, italicize Latin names of genera and species when used together, with the generic name in nominative singular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Felis leo; Rosa carolina; Conodecles favosus; Phyteuma halleri.' Note exceptions: botanical/geological guidelines differ slightly; medical matter generally prints such names in roman; astronomical conventions also differ and are specified (Greek/Latin/Arabic names italicized, catalogue designations, chemical element symbols, Fraunhofer line letters, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 72. Use 'Resolved.' in resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize and set the word 'Resolved.' in resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rule 39.

rubrics_metrics.name: 73. Use 'Continued' after headlines or 'To be continued' at article ends
rubrics_metrics.description: After headlines or titles use 'Continued' and use 'To be continued' at the end of articles when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: article footer '[To be continued]'. Cross-ref rule 179 for continuation handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: 74. Quotation marks for inline citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Put between quotation marks (roman type) citations run into the text of a passage from an author in his own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rule 85 for length considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 75. Quotation marks for consecutive quotations from different authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for quotations from different authors or different works by the same author when they follow each other uninterrupted by original matter or source references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rules 85-87 for reduced quotations and formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: 76. Quotation marks for word/phrase with definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks when a word or phrase is accompanied by its definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '"Drop-folio" means a page-number at the foot of the page.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 77. Quotation marks for unusual/technical/ironical words or phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Place quotation marks around unusual, technical, ironical, or otherwise notable words/phrases in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: usages like 'Her "five o'docks" were famous'; 'A "lead" is then inserted between the lines.' Also guidance when accompanied by words like 'so-called.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 78. Quotation marks for translations or English equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks around the English equivalent of a foreign word or phrase presented in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Weltanschauung, "world-view" or "fundamental aspect of life"; Mommsen Romische Geschichte ("History of Rome").'

rubrics_metrics.name: 79. Quotation marks to mark particular words called out
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks to single out the particular word(s) to which attention is directed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the term "lynch law"; the phrase "liberty of conscience"; the name "Chicago."'

rubrics_metrics.name: 80. Quotation marks for serial titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks around serial series titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '"English Men of Letters" series; "International Critical Commentary."'

rubrics_metrics.name: 81. Quotation marks for titles of shorter poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for titles of shorter poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Shelley's "To a Skylark."' (See rule 60 for longer works.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 82. Quotation marks for cited titles of subdivisions and other short works
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for cited titles of subdivisions (parts, books, chapters) and titles of papers, lectures, sermons, articles, toasts, mottoes, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The Beginnings of the Science of Political Economy Vol. I, "The British School," chap. ii, "John Stuart Mill"; the lecture was "Japan — Its Past, Present, and Future"; the toast "Our German Visitor".' Note: references to Preface, Introduction, Table of Contents, Index etc., of a specific work are set with capitals and without quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: 83. Quotation marks for names of ships
rubrics_metrics.description: Put ship names in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the U.S. SS. "Oregon."'

rubrics_metrics.name: 84. Quotation marks for titles of pictures and works of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for titles of pictures and works of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Muiiho's "The Holy Family."'

rubrics_metrics.name: 85. Reduced type for long quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Set in smaller type ordinary prose extracts of five or more lines and poetry citations of two or more lines; isolated prose quotations may be run into text if organically related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An isolated short quotation may be run in; where longer extracts are reduced maintain visual uniformity; see rule 86 for size reductions and rule 87 about omission of quotation marks on reduced citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 86. Specific point-size reductions for reduced citations
rubrics_metrics.description: When reducing type for citations, follow size-reduction conventions: from 11-pt and 10-pt reduce to 9-pt; from 9-pt to 8-pt; from 8-pt to 6-pt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rule 252 for more on typography.

rubrics_metrics.name: 87. Reduced citations normally omit quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced (smaller type) citations should not have quotation marks, except in cases noted in rule 75; quotation marks should also generally not be used in connection with italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions per rule 75; design considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 88. Quotation marks must include ellipses and 'etc.' where omission would be unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks should always include ellipses and 'etc.' when their inclusion clarifies that material has been omitted from the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate when 'etc.' belongs inside or outside quotes depending on whether it stands for omitted text within the quotation or additional material outside it.

rubrics_metrics.name: 89. Repeat opening quotation marks for broken quoted paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: If quoted prose broken into paragraphs, repeat the opening quotation marks at the beginning of each paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures clarity of continued quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 90. Clearing quotation marks for alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where alignment is desired, the quotation marks should be 'cleared' (project beyond the line of alignment) so the text aligns cleanly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided showing quotation marks projecting for alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: 91. Use double quotation marks for primary quotations, single for quotes within quotes, alternating thereafter
rubrics_metrics.description: Double quotation marks are used for primary quotations; single quotation marks for a quotation within a quotation, then alternate back and forth for further nesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative nested quotation example provided; follow sequence double → single → double → single, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 92. Spell out most civil and military titles preceding names
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out all civil and military titles and forms of address that precede names, except abbreviations Mr., Messrs., Mrs., Dr., Rev., Hon.; do not set 'the Rev.' or 'the Hon.' except in quotations; abbreviate Esq. following a name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: avoid using abbreviated forms for first names in running text; keep Esq. abbreviated after names.

rubrics_metrics.name: 93. Spell out Christian names and 'von' in ordinary text
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out Christian names (George, Charles, John) rather than abbreviations (Geo., Chas., Jno.), except in quoted matter or original signatures; spell out 'von' as part of a person's name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 240 for related guidance on names.

rubrics_metrics.name: 94. Spell out numbers of less than three digits in ordinary reading matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading matter, spell out numbers of less than three digits unless statistical/technical or in groups of six or more; exceptions apply for certain enumerations and technical contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'There are thirty-eight cities...' ; 'a fifty-yard dash'; but use figures for numbers in technical contexts, decimals, degrees, dimensions, enumerations, money, percentages, weights (examples given: 10°, 45 miles, 3 cubic feet, 24 pages, 100 bushels, 9 per cent, $1,000). Treat connected groups consistently (if largest has three or more digits use figures for all).

rubrics_metrics.name: 95. Spell out round numbers (approximate figures) in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Round (approximate) numbers should generally be spelled out (with limits specified) unless specific figures are given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The attendance was estimated at five hundred' (but write '550' if precise); 'a thesis of about three thousand words' (but use 'about 2,700' if specific). Use forms like 'fifteen hundred' rather than 'one thousand five hundred' for certain cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 96. Spell out numbers that begin a sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: All numbers, regardless of size, that commence a sentence should be spelled out in ordinary reading matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If impracticable, reconstruct sentence. Example provided: 'Five hundred and ninety-three men, 417 women...' or rewrite to 'The total number ... was 593 men.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 97. Spell out isolated sums of money in ordinary reading-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Sums of money occurring in isolated cases should be spelled out in ordinary reading matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The admission was two dollars.' When several amounts occur close together or in statistical contexts, use figures and currency symbols (e.g., 'Admission: men, $2; women, $1; children, 25 cents.').

rubrics_metrics.name: 98. Spell out time of day in ordinary prose; use figures in statistical/A.M.-p.m. contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter express times in words ('at four', 'at half-past two in the afternoon'); use figures statistically or with A.M./P.M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'at 4:15 P.M.' (omit 'o'clock' in such connections).

rubrics_metrics.name: 99. Express ages in words in ordinary prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Write ages in words in ordinary prose (e.g., 'eighty years and four months old'; 'children between six and fourteen').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard phrasing examples included.

rubrics_metrics.name: 100. Spell out names of centuries and similar numbered designations
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out numbers for centuries, Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, military bodies, political divisions, thoroughfares, etc., unless brevity is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'nineteenth century; Fifth Dynasty; Fifty-fourth Congress, Second Session; Fifth Avenue.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 101. References to particular decades
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to particular decades in lower-case spelled-out form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'in the nineties.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 102. Names of months spelled out except in statistical/long enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use full month names except in statistical matter or long enumerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'from January 1 to April 15' (omit ordinal suffixes like 'st, d, th' after dates).

rubrics_metrics.name: 103. Use 'United States' sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: 'United States' is generally spelled out except in quotations and certain connections (e.g., General Schofield, U.S.A.; U.S. SS. "Oregon"; footnotes and similar references where U.S. Geological Survey, etc. may be used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references to rules 22, 52, 106 for abbreviation conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 104. Capitalization of Railroad, Fort, Mount, Port in geographical names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Railroad', 'Fort', 'Mount', and 'Port' in geographical appellations as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad' (not 'R.R.' or 'Ry.'); 'Fort Wayne, Port Huron, Mount Elias.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 105. Generally spell out names of publications
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, spell out names of publications; this is flexible and may be modified by expediency, context, authoritative usage, and author's preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt, spell out — it's judged less offensive than abbreviating; no prescriptive list is possible; use good taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: 106. Abbreviate state names after towns with specified two- or three-letter forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviate names of states, territories, and possessions of the U.S. following town names using the listed abbreviated forms and without spaces between letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative list provided (Ala., Ariz., Ark., Cal., Colo., Conn., D.C., etc.). Cross-reference rules 22, 52, 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: 107. Abbreviate 'Company' and 'Brothers' in technical matter and use ampersand in firm names
rubrics_metrics.description: In technical matter (footnotes, bibliographies), abbreviate 'Company' and 'Brothers' and use '&' for 'and' in commercial firm names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The Macmillan Co., Macmillan & Co., Harper Bros.; Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad.' In running text not technical, spell out 'Company' and 'Brothers' if desired ('Harper Brothers have recently published ...').

rubrics_metrics.name: 108. Abbreviate 'Saint' as 'St.' in place names but omit for apostles/evangelists
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'St.' before certain place names (St. Louis, St. Peter's Church) but prefer omitting 'St.' before names of apostles, evangelists, and church fathers (Luke, Paul, Augustine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also use 'SS.' for plural saints (SS. Peter and Paul).

rubrics_metrics.name: 109. Standard abbreviations for books of the Bible and Apocrypha in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specified abbreviations for books of the Old and New Testaments, Apocrypha, and versions of the Bible commonly referred to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive lists given (Gen., Exod., Lev., Num., Deut., Matt., Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Rom., etc.) and abbreviations for versions (A.V., R.V., A.R.V., Vulg., LXX).

rubrics_metrics.name: 110. Abbreviations for literary references, volumes, numbers, pages and ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references, footnotes, and bibliographical matter, abbreviate 'volume', 'number', 'psalm', 'division', 'chapter', 'article', 'section', 'page', 'column', 'verse', 'line', 'note', 'figure' when followed by their number; use standard abbreviations for page ranges and continuations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Vol. I; No. 1; Ps. 20; chap. ii; art. iii; sec. 4; p. 5; col. 6; vs. 7; l. 8; n. 9; Fig. 7; pp. 5–7; pp. 5 f.; pp. 5 sff.' (See rules 37 and 237.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 111. (implicit) Symbols for metric units and common measures following numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use common metric symbols and measurement abbreviations following numerals where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '1 m., 2 dm., 3 cm., 4 mm.; cm. (=cubic meter), cc, gm. (=gram), gr. (=grain), h. (=hour), min. (=minute), sec. (=second); lb. (=pound), oz. (=ounce); yd., ft., in.; A.U. (=Angstrom units), H.P. (=horse-power),' etc. Cross-ref rule 123.

rubrics_metrics.name: 112. Follow original spelling/punctuation in quotations when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: In extracts from modern authors whose spelling/punctuation differ slightly, use office style; for Old English or where faithful rendering is essential, follow the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles must be accurately quoted; use discretion about keeping original orthography depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: 113. Form possessives of names ending in s or sibilant per syllable count
rubrics_metrics.description: For monosyllabic proper names ending in s or another sibilant, form possessive by adding '’s'; for multi-syllable names, add apostrophe alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'King James's Version, Burns's poems, Marx's theories; Moses' law, Jesus' birth, Demosthenes' orations, Berlioz' compositions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 114. Use 'a' before sounded h, long w, and 'one'
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sounded h, long w, and the word 'one' use 'a' as the indefinite article rather than 'an'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a hotel, a historical, a union, such a one.' Cross-ref rule 40.

rubrics_metrics.name: 115. Do not use ligatures in Latin quotations; retain ligatures in Old English and modern foreign languages where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid ligature 'oe' and 'ae' in quotations from Latin or anglicized derivatives; retain ligatures in Old English and in modern languages (French etc.) where the ligature is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: For Latin quotations separate letters; for Old English retain ligatures; examples from Aeneid and Balzac provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 116. Differentiate 'farther' and 'further'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Farther' for physical distance ('more remote'); 'further' for 'moreover' or 'in addition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the farther end; he went still farther; further, he suggested; a further reason.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 117. Use 'O' without comma for vocative; use 'Oh,' with comma for exclamation
rubrics_metrics.description: In forms of address (vocative), use 'O' without a comma following; for exclamations use 'Oh,' followed by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '"O thou most mighty ruler!"' vs '"Oh, why did not Cerberus drag me back to hell?"' Cross-ref rule 40.

rubrics_metrics.name: 118. Retain final e in certain participles ending with a vowel-starting syllable
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain participles retain the final 'e' in their primary word even though the participle begins with a syllable starting with a vowel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'agreeing, hieing, singeing, dyeing, hoeing, tingeing, eyeing, shoeing, vieing.' Also lists participles that omit the e (acknowledging, gluing, judging, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 119. Preferred American spellings list
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide preferred spellings for many commonly variant words in American English (long list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive examples given (e.g., 'abridgment, center, favor, kidnapper, accouter, check, fetish, Koran, acknowledgment, chiseled, fiber, labeled, adz, ... cannot' and more). Note: make one word of 'anyone', 'someone', 'everyone', 'today', 'tomorrow', 'tonight', 'cannot'. Distinguish 'sometimes' vs 'some time(s)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 120. Differentiate -ise and -ize endings per word lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify which verbs/words are spelled with -ise and which with -ize/-yze; a word-by-word prescribed list is provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two lists provided with many examples; e.g., '-ise': 'advertise, comprise, enterprise, premise, advise, compromise, excise, reprise, ...' ; '-ize': 'aggrandize, autolyze, civilize, energize, agonize, baptize, ...' Use the correct termination depending on the verb.

rubrics_metrics.name: 121. Punctuation font should match preceding word or letter
rubrics_metrics.description: All punctuation marks should be printed in the same style or font of type as the word or letter immediately preceding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '"With the cry of Banzai," the regiment stormed the hill'; ensure punctuation style consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: 122. Period marks the end of a complete sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a period to indicate the end of a complete sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rule 125 for exceptions and uses without a period.

rubrics_metrics.name: 123. Period after abbreviations except in certain technical cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a period after all abbreviations except where omission is mechanically necessary for mid-word omissions without recognized abbreviations; treat metric symbols as abbreviations but not chemical symbols or 'per cent' or book formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Macmillan & Co., Mr. Smith, St. Paul, No. 1, Chas.' ; exceptions listed for certain journals and for recognized abbreviations like IE, OE, AJSL, ZAW, CIL, and MS (no period). Cross-ref to rule 48 for special typographic practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: 124. No period after Roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the period after Roman numerals even when used as ordinals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Vol. IV; Louis XVI was on the throne.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 125. Omit period after running-heads, centered headlines, certain headings and signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a period after running-heads, centered headlines, side-heads set in separate lines, cut-in heads, box-heads in tables, superscriptions and legends that are not full sentences, date lines at top of communications, and after signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference rule 50 for date line guidance; see rules 279-283 for definitions of running-heads and related elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: 126. Period inside quotation marks and parentheses rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the period inside the quotation marks; place the period inside parentheses when enclosed matter is an independent sentence; otherwise place it outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a rule without exception for periods and quotation marks. Examples: 'Tennyson's "In Memoriam."' ; when parentheses form part of preceding sentence, period goes outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: 127. Use of exclamation point for outcry or emphatic/ironical utterance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the exclamation point to mark an outcry, emphatic statement, or ironical utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '"Long live the king!" "Heaven forbid!" "Good!" he cried; "How funny this seems!"' and admonitions about placement relative to quotation marks per rule 128.

rubrics_metrics.name: 128. Placement of exclamation point relative to quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the exclamation point inside quotation marks when it is part of the quotation; otherwise place it outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example contrasts given in rule 127 and 128.

rubrics_metrics.name: 129. Use interrogation point for direct queries; avoid in indirect questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the interrogation point for direct queries or to express doubt; do not use an interrogation point for indirect questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: direct: 'Who is this?' ; indirect: 'He asked whether he was ill.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 130. Interrogation point inside quotation marks only if part of quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the question mark inside quotation marks only when it is part of the quoted material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The question: "Who is who, and what is what?"' ; 'Were you ever in "Tsintsinnati"?'

rubrics_metrics.name: 131. Use of colon to mark greater discontinuity than semicolon and less than period
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a colon to mark a discontinuity greater than a semicolon and less than a period; commonly used to (i) emphasize close connection between two complete clauses, (ii) separate a complete clause from an illustrative/amplifying clause, (iii) introduce a formal statement, extract, or speech in dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrating each use and note that if the quotation is of a clause in the middle of a sentence, use a comma instead. Many illustrative quotes provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 132. Colon often substitutes for 'namely'/'as follows' and punctuation following such phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: A colon often implies 'namely,' 'as follows,' or similar; if such a word/phrase is used and what follows are complete clauses, follow it with a colon; otherwise use a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples contrast correct uses with 'viz.' and parenthetical dashes; guidance on punctuation with coordinating phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 133. Put a colon after salutatory phrase and introductory speaker remark
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a colon after the salutatory phrase at the beginning of a letter and after a speaker's introductory remark addressing chairman/audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'My dear Mr. Brown:' ; 'Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen:' (see rules 50 and 64).

rubrics_metrics.name: 134. Colon between chapter and verse in Scripture and between hours and minutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a colon to separate chapter and verse in Scripture passages and between hours and minutes in time indications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Matt. 2:5-13; 4:30 P.M.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 135. Colon between place of publication and publisher in bibliographical references
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon between place of publication and the publisher's name in bibliographical references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Clement of Alexandria (London: Macmillan), 11, 97.'
